catalog_quote: اما در گویش مورد نظر ما، یعنی در گویش اشتهارد که کلمات به دو دستهٔ مشخص مذکر و مؤنث تقسیم می‌شوند تنها واژه‌های مذکر حکم واژه‌های فارسی را دارند و تکیه‌شان بر هجای آخر است و واژه‌های مؤنث خود حکمی جداگانه دارند. ... در هر حال همهٔ اسم‌های مذکر مانند واژه‌های فارسی تکیه‌شان بر هجای آخر است مانند mardà (مرد)، furà (پسر)، zumâ (داماد)، dâhi (دایی)، qâhin (پدرزن) ... اما اسم‌های مؤنث (چه مؤنث حقیقی و چه مجازی) همه بدون استثناء مختوم به مصوت «-َ» a می‌باشند و باز همه بدون استثناء تکیه‌شان، برخلاف اسم‌های مذکر، در هجای ماقبل آخر است؛ به عبارت دیگر مؤنث بودن اسم دو شرط دارد: یکی آنکه مختوم به فتحه یا مصوت «-َ» باشد دیگر آنکه تکیه بر هجای ماقبل آخر آن باشد مانند: zéna (زن در مقابل شوی)، zeniya (زن در مقابل مرد)، tetiya (دختر)، xâka (خواهر)، vàya (عروس)، qâhina (مادرزن)، xasrùa (مادرشوهر) ... البته این دو علامت که باید آنها را علامات تأنیث نامید هر دو لازم‌اند و پیداست که تکیه (accent) در این گویش نقشی مهم بر عهده دارد و در بازشناسی واژه‌های مؤنث حائز اهمیت بسیاری است مثلاً اسم مذکر jingâ (گوسالهٔ نر دوساله) از پنج واج ج/ی/ن/گ/آ ساخته شده و اسم مؤنث jinga (گل آفتاب گردان) نیز درست از همان پنج واج ساخته شده و تفاوت آنها تنها در تکیه‌گاه آنهاست

new_statements.quote: Feminine nouns are commonly marked by an unstressed -a, with the stress regularly falling on the penultimate syllable, e.g. Esh. xoza "sand", kila "farrow", jua "stream", guara "calf", geliiaka "young calf", laxia "branch", ara "millstone"; Xia. cela "spindle" [...] Tak. vu(y)a "water", kasuya "turtle", fareka "chicken", hoya "stream". [p. 243:] In the masc. nouns, the sg. obl. ends in an unstressed -e.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Only a partial statement: in Southern Tati including Eshtehardi, feminine nouns end in an unstressed -a so that stress falls on the penultimate syllable, i.e. on the last syllable of the stem; the masculine singular oblique -e is likewise unstressed. Together with the stress-marked Eshtehardi forms in Windfuhr's Iranica entry (taká, tak-ehāˊ, Hasán-e, zén-a vs zen-í-a) and the Takestani JIPA description (nouns generally ultimate except feminine-suffixed ones) this points to stem-final stress with a class of unstressed inflectional suffixes (fem. -a, obl. -e) and stressed ones (plural -hā); no source opened states a general rule for Eshtehardi.
new_statements.exceptions: Feminine -a and masc. sg. oblique -e are unstressed (so word-level stress is penultimate in those forms); Chali fem. nouns in -i have dropped the -a.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms in a short survey article covering eight Ramand dialects plus Eshtehardi; Esh. examples are given first. Not a phonology section; the full stress treatment presumably lies in Yar-Shater 1969, which could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted 1962 statement is made for the Southern Tati (Ramand) group with Eshtehardi (Esh.) given as the first example set; Yarshater treats Eshtehard as an extension of the Ramand Tati villages. Windfuhr's Iranica entry EŠTEHĀRDĪ is specific to esht1238 but gives only stress-marked forms, no rule. Taherkhani & Nelson 2024 describes the sister dialect Takestani (take1255), not Eshtehardi, and is used only as corroboration.

new_statements.translation: In any case all masculine nouns, like Persian words, have their stress on the last syllable, e.g. mardà 'man', furà 'son', zumâ 'son-in-law', dâhi 'maternal uncle', qâhin 'father-in-law' ... But feminine nouns (whether truly or grammatically feminine) all without exception end in the vowel -a, and again all without exception have their stress, unlike masculine nouns, on the penultimate syllable; in other words, a noun's being feminine has two conditions: one, that it end in fatha, i.e. the vowel -a; the other, that the stress be on its penultimate syllable, e.g. zéna 'wife (vs. husband)', zeníya 'woman (vs. man)', tetíya 'daughter', xâka 'sister', váya 'bride'. [p. 316] Further, pp. 315-316: 'in the dialect of Eshtehard, where words divide into two distinct classes, masculine and feminine, only the masculine words behave like Persian words and have their stress on the last syllable, while the feminine words have a rule of their own.' pp. 316-317: 'it is evident that stress (accent) plays an important role in this dialect ... e.g. the masculine noun jingà "two-year-old bull calf" is built of the five phonemes j/i/n/g/a, and the feminine noun jínga "sunflower" is built of exactly the same five phonemes, and they differ only in the place of stress; likewise mâyà "leaven" vs. mâya, mivà "fruit" vs. míva "vine", and many others.' pp. 323-324: 'in the past-tense verb forms the feminine form carries the same markers as feminine nouns, i.e. the vowel -a at the end of the word and word stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g. arxóta "she slept", bekáta "she fell", ugahésta "she returned" (masc. arxot, bekat, ugahest)' and '[with masc. forms in -u] the two feminine markers (i.e. word-final -a and stress on the penultimate syllable) are added: beymù "he came" / beymíya "she came", bešu / bešíya, dešu / dašíya.' p. 328: 'all feminine nouns, when they stand as the head of an ezafe, change their ending: the short vowel -a becomes long -â, but the stress stays on their penultimate syllable, e.g. eštârda > eštârdâ (eštârdâ âwa "the water of Eshtehard"), âwa > âwâ (âwâ ringa "the colour of water"), naniya > naniyâ (naniyâ sadâ "mother's voice").'

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's existing statement (Yarshater 1962 p. 242: feminine nouns marked by unstressed -a with stress regularly on the penultimate syllable) and adds: (i) the explicit default, final stress on masculine nouns and on Persian-type words; (ii) the same two markers (-a + penult) on feminine past-tense verb forms and on the 3sg feminine copula/verb pairs; (iii) retention of penult stress under the ezafe-head allomorph -â; (iv) gender minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone; (v) a statement that the rule is exceptionless for feminines. Nothing contradicts the catalog. The catalog 'rule' field for Eshtehardi is empty and can be filled from this work together with Yarshater 19…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the final syllable, as in Persian: all masculine nouns (mardà, furà, zumâ, dâhi, qâhin), masculine past-verb forms (arxót, bekát, beymù) and Persian-type words. The feminine marker -a (on nouns, whether natural or grammatical gender, and on feminine past-tense verb forms) is never stressed, so every feminine word carries penultimate stress (zéna, zeníya, tetíya, xâka, váya, qâhína, xasrúa; arxóta, bekáta, beymíya); the penult stress is kept when the ezafe-head allomorph -â replaces -a (eštârdâ âwa). Because the same segmental string can be masculine or feminine, stress alone distinguishes pairs such as jingà 'bull calf' vs jínga 'sunflower', mâyà 'leaven' vs mâya, mivà 'fruit' vs míva 'vine', so the author calls stress (تکیه, accent) contrastive and one of the two obligatory markers of the feminine. (The catalog's older free-text reading 'morphologically determined' names the same fact from the other side: placement is predictable from gender, which is morphology.)
new_statements.exceptions: The whole feminine class is the systematic exception to final stress (penult, 'without exception'). The author also notes for Persian, not Eshtehardi, that vocatives (bâbâ, ardovân) take initial stress and that Yazdi has non-final stress (p. 315); no such vocative statement is made for Eshtehardi. Minimal pairs by gender (jingà/jínga, mâyà/mâya, mivà/míva) show stress is not predictable from the segments alone.
new_statements.identity_note: Nakhaʿi describes specifically the dialect of the town of Eshtehard (Karaj county, southwest of Tehran; he states its population as about 7,000 and calls it گویش اشتهارد), while remarking that the same gender system survives in the Tati dialects of the Qazvin villages (Buin, Sagzabad, Ebrahimabad, Danesfahan, Khoznin, Khiyarah, Shal, Esfarvarin, Siadehen, Takestan) and of other Karaj villages (Palangabad, Nekujar, Jaru, Sehatabad, Morad-tappeh); all example forms in the paper are Eshtehardi. The handwritten catalogue note on the scan's p. 312 header reads (partly legible) 'انتشارات دانشکدهٔ ادبیات و علوم انسانی ۱۱ - صص ۳۱۳-۳۲۵.. ۱۳۵۰', suggesting the proceedings volume appeared in 1350 SH (= 1971/72); the article itself prints no date or editor.

Only stress-related sentence: 'In nominals in stressed -á, masculine oblique -e > í; plural direct -ehāˊ > -hāˊ, feminine -á + ā > -ía (note doublets like zén-a "wife," zen-í-a "woman").' Stress-marked forms throughout (gāˊw-a, ríš-a, Maryám-a, lazák-a, taká, tak-ehāˊ, Hasán-e, arbāˊb-i-a) are consistent with stem-final stress, unstressed fem. -a and obl. -e, stressed plural -hā.
